 St. Paul Public Schools Board postpones staff reduction vote
 Ellen Galles and Richard Reeve KSTP 
 --> 
 St. Paul Public Schools Board delays staff reduction vote
 A rally in St. Paul pushed to stop midyear job cuts at public schools before the school board voted Tuesday night to delay the vote until next week.
 Teachers and families gathered before Tuesday night’s St. Paul Public Schools Board of Education meeting, where members discussed possible cuts. The district said the layoffs are tied to an unexpected enrollment drop after Operation Metro Surge.
District data presented at the meeting shows that St. Paul Public Schools has 542 fewer English language learners, or EL students, this year than originally projected. The district said Operation Metro Surge is one of the main reasons, and the decline in EL students is leading to a revenue loss of nearly $5 million this year.
To make up for that, the district is proposing cutting 16 EL teacher positions. The president of the St. Paul Federation of Educators said midyear cuts like this are rare and disruptive.
“Our EL students are students who have to be vulnerable in the classroom, and we work to help them feel comfortable with classmates and teachers,” Carrie Kyung, the president of the St. Paul Federation of Educators, said. “When you take away that teacher, you take away all that security for students.”
5 EYEWITNESS NEWS asked the district what happened to the 542 students who did not come back this year, including whether they transferred or where they are. The district said it does not have that data readily available.
 By state law, parents don’t need to inform a district where they are moving, but a district needs to make a good-faith effort to try to find out.
 St. Paul schools may cut 16 teachers after enrollment drop
 Late Tuesday night, the board voted unanimously to postpone the vote on staffing reductions to no later than Oct. 30; however, it could be as early as Oct. 26.
 Parents and teachers pushed back on those cuts at the meeting after learning the layoff notices would’ve gone out on Wednesday, drawing jeers from those in attendance.
 Many at the meeting said it’s unfair to offset the budget gap by eliminating teacher jobs.
 “Let’s not overlook the message this sends to families. None of you showed up, so we had to terminate people, but if you do show up, we won’t have staff to support you,” said Hilies Scully, an SPPS teacher.
 “After the targeted violence against immigration communities during Operation Metro Surge, I find it unconscionable that the board would consider cutting these same teachers, who have time and time again proven essential to the well-being of our students,” added Eric, an SPPS parent.
 “Last school year, many of our young students were emotionally traumatized after being hunted by ICE. Many of them missed months of school, but they came back to us,” said SPPS teacher Christie Herman Hall.
